transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-09-29 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Liam Carter, Priya Kapoor, Noah Ruiz (Redwood) / Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Sara Bloom, Tom Reed (Parallax Financial)

Summary:
Quick hands-on console walkthrough focused on stitching request logs, the journey map UI, and error analysis for the intermittent model-timeout/fallbacks ParallaxFin has been seeing. Demo included playback of a failing request, KV-cache hit/miss visualization, and how automatic fallbacks route to smaller model variants. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics covered:
- Console journey map and timeline stitching
- Request inspector and raw payload access (PII handling discussed)
- KV cache hits/misses and prefix caching behavior
- Model fallback and routing policies (hosted vs dedicated implications)
- Telemetry export and SOC2/audit log access

Action items (high level):
- Share security pack and network diagram
- Parallax to supply sample request IDs for reproduction
- Redwood to propose pilot config and pricing

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Liam from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Today Priya and Noah will demo a few console flows — stitching request journeys, digging into a failing inference, and showing the fallback routing. Maya, can you give a quick one-liner on the issue you folks are seeing?
[00:18] Maya Chen: Yeah thanks Liam. Uh we see intermittent timeouts for our chat assistant when loads spike, usually around 90 to 120 seconds into a session, and sometimes the response switches to a lower-quality model without tracing why. We want to be able to replay an exact request and see where latency piled up — whether it was in the network, in the KV cache, or during decode.
[00:35] Priya Kapoor: Great, so we'll start with the journey map which stitches together the request logs, traces, and console events. I should warn the transcription may mess up some product names, you know how it goes.
[00:45] [01:02] Priya Kapoor: Ok pulling up the Parallax demo workspace — here you can see the session timeline on the left, heatmap for latency, and a list of requests. I'm going to filter for the request id Maya sent earlier, uh that one looks like pxf-7a3b-... Missed last char there, sorry.
[01:25] Diego Alvarez: that's the one, we pasted a batch of ids into the support ticket.
[01:30] Priya Kapoor: Perfect. So the journey map stitches three things: the request ingress, the runtime token loop traces, and any external KV/cache events. Notice this spike at 00:00:12 on the timeline — you can click into the span.
[01:48] [02:10] Priya Kapoor: Here in the span view you can see per-step timing: queue time 8ms, model init 1.2s, kv lookup 0.03s, decode 23.4s, and then a big gap labelled 'wait-for-kv-refresh' — that's suspicious.
[02:28] Tom Reed: Wait-for-kv-refresh, is that a Redwood internal name? We have similar naming in our infra and want to ensure it's mappable.
[02:36] Noah Ruiz: Yeah it maps to the runtime event where the KV cache misses and triggers a background refresh from the persistent store; sometimes the refresh can block subsequent requests if the cache is pinned incorrectly.
[02:55] Priya Kapoor: There's also an annotation that the fallback policy fired at the 32s mark, so the request was rerouted to the small-quantized variant. That explains the change in quality.
[03:10] Maya Chen: The tricky part is the reroute isn't always obvious from our logs because we aggregate per-minute; the console timeline gives per-request visibility which is good.
[03:22] [03:40] Priya Kapoor: Right — let me switch to request inspector which shows the raw payload, headers, and model selection history. Note: for privacy we mask any PII in the payload unless you enable raw exports.
[03:53] Priya Kapoor: Here you can see model: rdx-llamax-13b (primary), fallback to rdx-llamax-7b at 00:00:32, and the routing reason: 'latency-budget-exceeded'.
[04:10] Sara Bloom: Can we see why the latency budget was exceeded? Is it purely CPU/GPU contention or network?
[04:17] Priya Kapoor: Good question. The timeline shows the decode step ballooned; if you look at the node map on the right, the request hit a node with lower free-GPU-memory due to another high-token session. Redwood has a few levers: we surface node-level metrics here, and you can set per-route SLOs to prefer latency over cost or vice versa.
[04:38] [05:00] Noah Ruiz: Also, automatic batching could increase tail latency in certain workloads. You can adjust the batching window per-route; we recommend a smaller window for chat-style interactive use.
[05:14] Tom Reed: How do you recommend we set that? We need sub-300ms median for our concierge flow.
[05:20] Priya Kapoor: For sub-300ms median you should set batching window to 5-10ms and enable prefix KV caching; we can push a suggestion from Redwood Optimize after we see token distribution.
[05:35] [06:00] Diego Alvarez: On the KV cache: you mentioned prefix caching — we've got a lot of similar prefixes across sessions, will that blow up memory?
[06:12] Priya Kapoor: The console shows estimated memory per-prefix and retention policies. Also there's an eviction policy chart — LRU with sampling. If you want more aggressive eviction, you can set max prefixes per-tenant.
[06:28] [06:45] Priya Kapoor: I'm going to play back the failing request now — console playback will re-run the request against a trace simulator but flagged as a dry run, so no external side-effects.
[06:55] [07:20] *playback starts*
[07:22] [07:40] Priya Kapoor: Playback shows the same decode hang. I'm going to toggle on 'node debug' which surfaces node-level logs — ah we see repeated 'kv-refresh-timeout' errors on that node.
[07:57] Maya Chen: That matches our prod traces where we saw a small percentage of 'kv timeouts' but couldn't link them to specific requests.
[08:10] Priya Kapoor: Right — that's the power of request mapping. You can drill from the high-level SLO to the exact trace and then to node logs.
[08:22] [09:00] Liam Carter: Quick compliance question — for audit purposes we need immutable logs and an export that matches our SIEM. How do you handle that?
[09:10] Priya Kapoor: We support audit-log exports to S3, and you can configure retention and immutability via object-lock. For SOC2 customers we also provide signed event digests and an audit bundle. I'll add the SOC2 pack to the next steps.
[09:27] [10:05] Diego Alvarez: What about KMS/HSM integration? We keep keys in our HSM and need to ensure requests never leave the VPC in raw form.
[10:14] Noah Ruiz: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and optionally an on-prem inference pack. For Hosted we do envelope encryption and KMS integration; we can provide region restrictions and a private control plane in VPC peering mode.
[10:33] [11:00] Priya Kapoor: Back to the workflow: you can set an automatic fallback policy with a frequency cap — e.g., only fallback after 2 consecutive timeouts — and you can instrument a canary cohort. That prevents noisy single failures from downgrading every session.
[11:20] [11:45] Priya Kapoor: Another useful view is 'token heatmap' which correlates token position with latency. See this request — latency spikes at token 512 where the model does a long-form planning step.
[11:58] Sara Bloom: That's interesting, our prompts do often trigger planning sequences mid-session. Is there a way to force a cached plan or warm the model?
[12:10] Priya Kapoor: Yes, prefix caching or pre-warming calls can help. Redwood Optimize can recommend which prompts to cache based on observed repetition. We'll run a prompt-pattern analysis during the pilot.
[12:28] [12:50] Liam Carter: I know this is getting technical, but can we show how traces look when there's a network egress problem?
[12:58] Priya Kapoor: Sure — switching to an example where the node had intermittent egress errors. The journey map shows a 'network backoff' annotation and the trace contains the underlying socket retry logs. See the repeated 'connection reset' entries at the 2-3 second mark.
[13:20] Tom Reed: Could that be our VPC NAT gateway or something on your side?
[13:28] Noah Ruiz: It could be either; that's why the console correlates our node metrics with your VPC flow logs if you enable the integration. We can surface the matching src/dst connection and the nat IP for cross-checking.
[13:46] [14:10] Priya Kapoor: Ok quick sidebar on sampling — by default we sample high-latency traces and error traces at 100% and low-latency at 1%. You can adjust the sampling policy per-route if you want more coverage.
[14:30] Maya Chen: We want 100% for the concierge route for at least two weeks during onboarding.
[14:38] Liam Carter: We can do that for the pilot. We'll capture everything for that route and then roll back after the initial period.
[14:48] [15:10] Priya Kapoor: I'm going to open the fallback policy editor — you can create policies based on per-route metrics, e.g., fallback if p95 > 2s for 3 consecutive minutes, and you can define fallback targets (model small/quantized, different region, or queue to burst capacity).
[15:30] Diego Alvarez: If we fallback to a different region, does that violate data residency?
[15:36] Priya Kapoor: Good catch — you can restrict fallback options to only same-region or same-tenant to avoid crossing boundaries. We also surface a compliance warning if a selected fallback would route data out of a compliant region.
[15:52] [16:10] Noah Ruiz: Also note the cost panel shows the unit cost delta when fallbacks occur; it's explicit so you can trade off quality vs cost.
[16:22] [16:50] Priya Kapoor: Alright I'm going to demonstrate a quick workflow for 'failed request forensic' — start from the error spike, jump to the list of affected request ids, then bulk-download traces and share a permalink with your engineers.
[17:10] Sara Bloom: That's super helpful, previously our ops would have to grep logs across services.
[17:20] [17:40] Priya Kapoor: There's a 'correlation hash' included with each trace that you can ingest into your observability pipeline so links remain stable across exports.
[17:52] Maya Chen: How does retention work, we have regulatory constraints about storing transcripts for more than 90 days?
[17:58] Priya Kapoor: Retention policy is configurable per-tenant; we can set a 90-day max and also provide auto-redaction for transcripts older than X days.
[18:10] [18:40] Liam Carter: Let's do a quick failure reproducibility test — Priya, replay the trace but force the node to simulate low-memory to reproduce the decode hang.
[18:52] Priya Kapoor: Doing that now — toggling the 'simulate node condition' flag — the playback now shows decode time shooting up and then the fallback after the threshold.
[19:10] [19:40] Diego Alvarez: That simulation helps a lot. Can you capture the exact node image and runtime config? We want to mirror it in our staging.
[19:52] Priya Kapoor: Yes the playback includes a 'runtime snapshot' link — it lists kernel versions, quantization settings, and the batch window used. I'll attach that in the export.
[20:05] [20:40] Liam Carter: Security question from legal: do you keep raw request payloads in logs for hosted mode?
[20:50] Priya Kapoor: By default we store masked transcripts and the raw payloads are encrypted and accessible under strict access controls; for enterprises we can turn on tenant-managed KMS and restrict raw export privileges.
[21:08] [21:40] Priya Kapoor: Switching back to the console, here's the 'error analysis' pane which aggregates top error classes and the top affected routes. You can click into the top error 'kv-refresh-timeout' and see a histogram, top nodes, and a linked list of sample traces.
[21:58] Tom Reed: Are those histograms adjustable by time-range and percentile?
[22:05] Priya Kapoor: Yes, slide the time-window and toggle p50/p95/p99. You can also save a view as a dashboard tile.
[22:25] [22:50] Maya Chen: I noticed earlier you mentioned 'signed event digests' — is that compatible with our SIEM ingest?
[22:58] Noah Ruiz: We produce a JSONL audit bundle and a signed manifest; most SIEMs can ingest the JSON lines and verify the manifest. We'll map fields with your vendor during the pilot.
[23:12] [23:40] Priya Kapoor: Ok last demo piece — 'bulk explain' for a failing test set: you can paste a list of request ids and run a batch analysis which will produce a CSV with columns for model, latency, fallback_reason, node_id, and a suggested remediation tag.
[23:58] Sara Bloom: The remediation tags sound great, are they auto-generated?
[24:05] Priya Kapoor: They're heuristics from Redwood Optimize — many are simple (increase batching window, enable prefix cache, move to dedicated). We also show confidence levels.
[24:20] [24:50] Maya Chen: For the pilot, we want to try Dedicated for the concierge route and Hosted for everything else. What does that split look like operationally?
[24:58] Liam Carter: We can do hybrid at route level — dedicated pool assigned to route A, hosted for others. Dedicated gets you pinned GPUs and isolation, hosted gives elastic burst. We'll propose a commit size for Dedicated based on your peak qps.
[25:18] [25:50] Diego Alvarez: If we go Dedicated, can we still use the console's tracing and playback?
[25:58] Priya Kapoor: Yes, the console abstracts the deployment model — same telemetry, same playback features; data plane runs in your dedicated pool but control plane traces are visible in your private console.
[26:15] [26:40] Tom Reed: Any difference in latency when using dedicated vs hosted?
[26:46] Noah Ruiz: Dedicated avoids noisy-neighbor variability so tail latency improves; however if you underprovision the pool you'll see queuing. We'll recommend autoscaling heads and burst capacity to balance cost.
[27:05] [27:30] Priya Kapoor: I'm going to export a small forensic bundle for the sample ids Maya gave — you'll see a permalink in the chat.
[27:45] [28:05] *export generates link*
[28:08] Priya Kapoor: Link is up: https://console.redwood.ai/r/exports/ff-demo-parallax-20250929 (example link, access controlled)
[28:22] Maya Chen: Got it, seeing it now.
[28:30] [28:58] Liam Carter: Let's run rapid Q/A — Sara?
[29:05] Sara Bloom: Quick question: do you support SAML SSO and RBAC mapping to our AD groups?
[29:12] Priya Kapoor: Yes SAML/SSO with group mapping and role-based permissions are supported; we also have audit trails per-user.
[29:22] Tom Reed: On the networking front, we need to ensure egress IPs are stable for allow-listing.
[29:30] Noah Ruiz: For Hosted we publish an IP range for our egress; for Dedicated we can either publish an assigned NAT IP or support VPC peering so you can manage egress.
[29:46] [30:10] Diego Alvarez: Any limits on log export throughput? We might push tens of GB per day during onboarding.
[30:18] Priya Kapoor: We handle high-throughput exports; for large volumes we recommend streaming to an S3 ingestion pipeline with multipart and lifecycle rules.
[30:32] [31:00] Maya Chen: Ok can you summarize what Redwood needs from us to get a pilot going?
[31:08] Liam Carter: Sure — high level: 1) one route definition for the concierge flow, 2) sample request ids and token distribution, 3) security contacts and preferred KMS model, 4) target SLOs. We'll spin up a pilot config and share pricing.
[31:25] [31:42] Priya Kapoor: I'll also add Optimize's recommendations once we ingest token histograms — that will include batching/window suggestions and prefix cache candidate list.
[31:55] [32:20] Sara Bloom: How long does the pilot typically last?
[32:26] Liam Carter: Standard is 2-4 weeks to get baseline metrics, but can be shorter if your team has a tight timeline.
[32:34] [33:00] Maya Chen: We want something actionable in two weeks.
[33:08] Liam Carter: We can do a 2-week focused pilot for the concierge route.
[33:18] [33:40] Priya Kapoor: Quick note: we saw a small discrepancy between how your team called the KV component (you said "cache service") and how our runtime labels it. We'll include a mapping doc so your logs translate cleanly into console fields.
[33:58] Diego Alvarez: appreciate that.
[34:10] [34:40] Noah Ruiz: Last demo: illustrating how automatic rollouts work — when we push a model variant you can configure a canary percentage, health checks, and automatic rollback if quality/regression alerts fire.
[34:58] Tom Reed: Do those regression alerts tie into our evals?
[35:05] Priya Kapoor: Yes they can — we integrate with your evaluation sets and run a smoke comparison on every rollout. If the quality delta exceeds your threshold, rollback happens automatically.
[35:22] [35:50] Maya Chen: That's crucial for us.
[35:56] [36:20] Liam Carter: We're about 15 minutes left — any remaining blockers?
[36:28] Maya Chen: Just clarity on pricing for dedicated commit vs expected ROI.
[36:34] Liam Carter: I'll send a tailored pricing sheet showing the unit economics with and without prefix caching and with a suggested commit size.
[36:44] [37:10] Priya Kapoor: I'll follow up on the SOC2 and network diagram and also attach the runtime snapshot for the simulated failing node.
[37:22] Sara Bloom: We'll pull together the sample request ids and a redacted support bundle.
[37:30] [37:58] Maya Chen: One more question — can the console show end-user session anonymized identifiers so we can correlate to our product analytics?
[38:08] Priya Kapoor: Yes, with hashing/PSI techniques we can provide stable anonymous ids for correlation. That's configurable.
[38:22] [38:50] Diego Alvarez: Any competitor gotchas we should be aware of? We considered building our own stack and looked at OtherAIEndpoints.
[38:58] Liam Carter: Main trade-offs: building in-house gives control but long-term ops cost. Other vendors often limit visibility into node-level traces or charge high egress for full trace exports. We'll include a comparison note.
[39:16] [39:40] Priya Kapoor: Ok wrapping up — I'll list the concrete next steps in the chat and assign action items.
[39:50] [40:10] Liam Carter: Thanks all, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the pilot config and SOC2 pack.
[40:18] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, this was very useful.
[40:25] Tom Reed: Thanks.
[40:30] [41:00] End of recording.
